script.opening: (Mother, angry and defensive, waving the letter; Kai beside her looking at the floor.) "I'll be honest, I'm fuming. The school sent this letter saying Kai's 'obese' — obese! He's just a growing boy, he's not fat. I feel like they're calling me a bad mother. And now he's upset about it. I almost didn't come. What are you going to say — put a 9-year-old on a diet?"

facts.text: National Child Measurement Programme letter, Year 5 equivalent: says Kai is "very overweight". Will hold it up to the camera: height 140 cm, weight 47 kg (above the 98th centile for BMI).
(Kai, looking down, if asked kindly) "Sometimes. A couple of kids" — called names at break time. "He's always been one of the taller ones. No problems at school with his work."

"Not that I've noticed" — no snoring or stopping breathing at night, no joint or hip pain, no excessive thirst or passing urine, no headaches. No dark velvety skin patches. Growing taller steadily. No medicines (no steroids). No allergies.

"We're busy. Everyone's at work or school, we eat what's quick, he's on his tablet a fair bit. We drive most places. It's not like we live on chips." Fizzy drinks most days, takeaway twice a week, crisps in his lunchbox. Tablet 3–4 hours a day; bedtime about 10 pm.
(Kai) "Football. I like football." Plays at lunchtime; stopped after-school club when Mum's shifts changed.
Mum works shifts in a warehouse; Dad drives a delivery van. Older sister, 14. Dad has type 2 diabetes; Mum describes herself as "big-boned". No social worker.
"That I've failed him. That everyone's judging me. I just want him to be happy — I don't want him obsessing about food."

Defensive at first: "Fine. As long as nobody's having a go." Softens if the doctor avoids blame and words like "fat", acknowledges her feelings and involves Kai. If the doctor lectures or talks about Kai's weight bluntly in front of him, get angry and threaten to leave. Asks: "So the letter might be wrong?" Offers her own idea: "Maybe water instead of fizzy drinks. And he could do football after school more." Kai brightens when football is mentioned.

ice.ideas: "He's just a growing boy — the letter is wrong and judging me."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — shame and guilt at being seen as a bad mother; Kai being teased; fear of making him obsess about food. Underneath, Dad's diabetes worries her.
ice.expectations: "To know if he's actually alright" — and not to be told off or have her son put on a diet.

cues: "They're calling me a bad mother." — the shame behind the anger.
"Now he's upset about it." — Kai's feelings and possible bullying.
"Put a 9-year-old on a diet?" — invites a whole-family, no-diet approach.

checkpoints.text: Handles the topic with ZERO blame and compassion — acknowledges the mother’s feelings, is mindful of the CHILD in the room (avoids "fat"/blame) and protects his self-esteem

Assesses objectively with BMI CENTILE for age/sex on a UK90 growth chart (not adult BMI; ≥91st overweight, ≥98th obesity — NICE NG246), arranging face-to-face measurement and plotting trajectory to ground the conversation in data

Considers/excludes secondary causes (endocrine/genetic — often with short stature/delay) and screens COMORBIDITY at or above the 98th centile (BP, glucose/HbA1c and lipids, acanthosis/insulin resistance, sleep apnoea, joints — NICE NG246) and crucially MOOD/bullying/self-esteem
Takes a WHOLE-FAMILY lifestyle history (diet, drinks, portions, activity, screen time, sleep, routines) without judgement, identifying achievable levers and readiness/circumstances

Manages as a FAMILY with small, specific, positive changes framed around health (maintain weight while growing rather than dieting a child), signposting to family weight-management/tier-2 services and the school nurse
Reads the anger as shame/guilt, allies WITH the family against the problem, and turns a defensive encounter into a supportive, hopeful plan
Protects and positively involves the child, checks the family’s understanding and readiness, and avoids stigmatising language throughout

Safety-nets and follows up: comorbidity follow-up, programme signposting, review of changes, attention to emotional/bullying impact and any safeguarding/neglect concern — non-shaming, whole-family care

worked.txt: "I can see that letter really upset you — and let me say clearly, I don’t think you’re a bad mum, and we’re not here to label or diet Kai. Let’s look at this together as a family thing, gently."

"For children we don’t use the adult measure — we plot growth on a chart for his age. I’d like the nurse to measure him properly this week and plot it, then I’ll show you where Kai sits and how he’s been tracking, so we’re working from facts, not just a scary word."

"If he’s tall and growing along his height line when we measure him, that reassures me there’s no hidden medical cause. The nurse will check his blood pressure too, and depending on the numbers I may suggest a blood test. (Gently, to Kai) How are you doing in yourself, mate — is anyone giving you a hard time at school?"
"Tell me about a normal day for the family — meals, drinks, getting about, screens, sleep. Not to judge — kids just do what the household does, so changes work best when everyone’s in."

"Let’s pick one or two easy wins as a family — maybe water instead of fizzy drinks, and a kickabout a couple more times a week. The goal isn’t a diet — it’s for Kai to grow into his weight and have more energy."

"There’s a friendly family programme I can refer you to, and the school nurse can help. Let’s review how it’s going. And if Kai’s being teased or it’s getting him down, tell me — that matters just as much."

f.learning: Childhood obesity is a sensitive, easily-shaming topic that must be handled with compassion and zero blame, especially with the child in the room: acknowledge the parent’s feelings, affirm you are not labelling them a bad parent, and be mindful of every word in front of the child — avoid "fat" and blame, and protect his self-esteem, because the tone determines whether the family engages. Assess objectively using BMI centile for age and sex on a UK90 growth chart (not adult BMI cut-offs; overweight at or above the 91st centile and obesity at or above the 98th, NICE NG246, 2025), measuring face to face — nothing can be measured on a video call — and plotting height, weight and trajectory to ground the conversation in data rather than the emotive letter. Most childhood obesity is lifestyle-related, but consider and exclude the uncommon secondary causes (endocrine such as hypothyroidism or Cushing’s, and genetic syndromes — typically with short stature, developmental delay or dysmorphism, so a tall child growing along his centiles is reassuring), and screen for comorbidity and complications (blood pressure, acanthosis nigricans/insulin resistance, glucose/HbA1c and lipids at or above the 98th centile, sleep apnoea, joint problems) and crucially for mood, bullying and self-esteem. Take a whole-family lifestyle history without judgement (meals, sugary drinks/snacks, portions, activity, screen time, sleep, routines), framing it as understanding rather than interrogating, and identify achievable levers and the family’s readiness and circumstances. Manage as a family rather than dieting a child: agree small, specific, positive changes framed around health, energy and growing well (children generally maintain weight while growing into it rather than losing weight), signpost to a family-based, multicomponent weight-management/tier-2 programme (NICE NG246) and school nurse, and keep the child positive and involved. The hidden agenda is anger masking shame, guilt and feeling judged, with possible bullying of the child; remove blame, ally with the family against the problem, protect the child, watch for emotional impact and — in extreme/neglect situations — any safeguarding concern.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG246 (2025) — Overweight and obesity management · NICE CG89 — Child maltreatment: when to suspect · National Child Measurement Programme (Office for Health Improvement and Disparities)
knowledge.summary: In children, weight is judged by BMI centile for age and sex, not adult cut-offs. Most childhood obesity reflects family-wide habits; secondary causes are rare and usually come with short stature or developmental delay. The management is family-based, positive and free of blame.

points.t: NICE NG246: use BMI centiles on UK90 charts in children, not adult BMI. Overweight is at or above the 91st centile; obesity at or above the 98th centile. Plot height and weight and look at the trajectory.

points.h: Look for a cause only when the pattern suggests one
points.t: Short stature or slowing height velocity, developmental delay, dysmorphic features, or very early-onset severe obesity suggest an endocrine or genetic cause and need paediatric assessment. A child who is growing along or above his height centile is reassuring.

NICE NG246: consider assessing comorbidities at or above the 98th centile — blood pressure, glucose and lipids, snoring and sleep apnoea, joint problems, acanthosis nigricans, and psychological wellbeing including bullying and low self-esteem.

NICE NG246: family-based, multicomponent lifestyle interventions — diet, physical activity and behaviour change — are the core. For many growing children the aim is to slow weight gain while height catches up, not to diet.
Use neutral, person-first language focused on health; avoid blame and avoid words that stigmatise, especially with the child present. Ask permission before discussing weight.
Weight alone is not a safeguarding issue. NICE CG89 applies only where there are wider concerns about neglect, such as failure to engage with care for serious obesity-related harm.

Snoring and apnoeas, hip or knee pain and limp, thirst and tiredness, growth pattern, mood and bullying.
Probable overweight or obesity on the school measurement, to be confirmed by centile and trajectory; no features of a secondary cause.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

model.text: Hello Mrs Pyle, and hello Kai. Thanks for coming. What would you like to talk about today?

I’ll be honest, I’m fuming. The school sent this letter saying Kai’s obese — obese! He’s just a growing boy. I feel like they’re calling me a bad mother, and now he’s upset. I almost didn’t come. What are you going to say — put a 9-year-old on a diet?

I can see that letter has really upset you both, and I’m glad you came anyway. Let me say straight away: I don’t think you’re a bad mum, and I’m not going to put Kai on a diet. Would it be okay to talk about what the letter means and whether there’s anything that would help Kai feel his best?
model.why: Defuses, removes blame, answers the diet fear and asks permission

model.text: Fine. As long as nobody’s having a go.
Nobody is. I’ll ask a few questions about how Kai is and your family’s routines, then explain how we look at growth in children, and we’ll decide together what, if anything, to do.
Kai, how are you doing in yourself? Is anyone giving you a hard time at school?
model.why: Checks the child’s wellbeing and bullying first

model.text: (Kai, looking down) Sometimes. A couple of kids.
Thank you for telling me, Kai. That’s not okay, and we’ll come back to it. Mrs Pyle, has he had any health problems — snoring or stopping breathing at night, sore knees or hips, or being very tired?
Not that I’ve noticed.
And how has he grown over the years — is he tall for his age, or has his height ever slowed down? Any worries about his development or learning?
model.why: Screens for red flags of a secondary cause

model.text: He’s always been one of the taller ones. No problems at school with his work.
That’s helpful. Could you talk me through a normal day for the family — meals, drinks, how you get about, screens, bedtime? I ask everyone this; it’s about understanding, not judging.
model.why: Whole-family lifestyle history framed without blame

model.text: We’re busy. Everyone’s at work or school, we eat what’s quick, he’s on his tablet a fair bit. We drive most places. It’s not like we live on chips.
That sounds like most busy families. Is there anything he really enjoys doing that gets him moving?
model.why: Normalises and looks for positive levers

model.text: (Kai) Football. I like football.
Mrs Pyle, when you read that letter, what went through your mind?
model.why: Explores the feelings under the anger

model.text: That I’ve failed him. That everyone’s judging me. I just want him to be happy — I don’t want him obsessing about food.
Wanting him to be happy and relaxed about food is exactly the right goal, and it’s one we share. So what would you like to get out of today?
model.why: Allies with the mother’s values and elicits expectations

model.text: I suppose to know if he’s actually alright.

For children we don’t use the adult measure. We plot height and weight on a chart for his age and see how he’s tracking over time. I’d like the nurse to measure him properly this week, check his blood pressure, and plot it all so we’re working from facts rather than a label in a letter.
model.why: BMI centile, objective measurement and BP — arranged face to face

model.text: So the letter might be wrong?

The school measurement is usually accurate, but it’s a single snapshot. What matters is the pattern. And if he’s tall and growing well along his height line, that reassures me there isn’t a hidden medical cause. Depending on the numbers, I may suggest a blood test too.
model.why: Explains secondary-cause reasoning and conditional tests

model.text: Okay. That seems fair.

The goal isn’t a diet. For a growing boy, it’s about habits the whole family shares, so that he grows into his weight and has more energy. What’s one or two small changes that would feel easy for your family?
Maybe water instead of fizzy drinks. And he could do football after school more.
Those are brilliant. Kai, how does more football sound?
(Kai) Good.

There’s also a local family programme — it’s fun, active and for the whole family, not a weight class. Would you like me to refer you? And I’d like to speak to school about the teasing, with your permission, and the school nurse can support Kai too.
model.why: Signposts family weight-management support and addresses bullying

model.text: Yes to both. I didn’t know school had a nurse who’d help.

So: the nurse measures Kai and checks his blood pressure this week, we look at the chart together, water instead of fizzy drinks and more football, the family programme, and school about the teasing. Does that sound right?
Yes. It’s a lot better than I expected.

Please come back sooner if Kai starts snoring loudly or stopping breathing at night, gets very thirsty or tired, or has pain in his hips or knees or starts limping. And Kai — if the teasing gets worse or you feel down about it, tell your mum or tell me. That matters just as much.
model.why: Specific safety-net for comorbidity and emotional harm

model.text: (Kai nods.) Mum: Thank you. I came in ready for a fight.
You came in because you care about him. We’re on the same side.

social.t: Children living with obesity are often teased. Bullying harms mental health and reduces activity; it deserves its own plan with school.
Time pressure, cost of food and activities, and access to safe places to play shape what is achievable. Ask, and fit the plan to the family.

legal.t: NICE CG89: obesity alone is not a safeguarding concern. Consider neglect only where there are wider concerns, such as persistent failure to engage with care for serious obesity-related harm.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): ask the parent’s agreement before contacting school about bullying, and share only what is needed.
Person-first, health-focused language and asking permission to discuss weight are part of treating patients with respect (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

community.t: Local family-based child weight-management programmes (tier 2) and the school nurse; the National Child Measurement Programme letter usually lists local support.

redFlags: Short stature, falling height centile, developmental delay or dysmorphism — endocrine or genetic cause, paediatric assessment
Loud snoring with apnoeas, hip or knee pain with a limp (SUFE), thirst and polyuria
Low mood, bullying, self-harm or disordered eating
psychosocial: Family routines: meals, drinks, screens, transport, sleep
Kai’s experience at school and his self-esteem
ice: Idea: “He’s just a growing boy — the letter is wrong”
Concern: being judged as a bad mother; Kai being put on a diet or obsessing about food
Expectation: to know whether he is actually alright

playbook.diagnosis: Possible overweight or obesity on a school measurement, to be confirmed by BMI centile on UK90 charts with height trajectory. No features of a secondary cause; comorbidity assessment if at or above the 98th centile.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “For children we don’t use the adult measure. We plot height and weight on a chart for his age, and what matters is how he’s tracking over time — not one number in a letter.”

management.reflectIce: “You want Kai to be happy and relaxed about food — that’s exactly our goal too. Nobody here is judging you as a mum.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around the family’s time and budget, Kai’s love of football, and the bullying, which needs its own action with school.
sharedPlan: Nurse appointment: height, weight, BMI centile on UK90 charts, blood pressure
One or two family-chosen changes (water instead of fizzy drinks; more football)
Referral to a family weight-management programme; school and school nurse about teasing
safetyNet: Snoring with pauses in breathing, limp or hip or knee pain, thirst or tiredness — come back sooner
Low mood or worsening bullying — tell us; review after the measurements

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on words, not knowledge. A candidate who knows the centile thresholds still fails if the mother feels blamed or Kai hears himself described as fat.

items.fail: Arguing with the mother about whether the letter is right.
items.why: Defending the school puts you on the opposite side; the anger is shame and fear of judgement.
items.fix: Name her feelings, say clearly she is not a bad mum, and ask permission to talk about it.

items.fail: Talking about Kai’s weight in the third person while he sits there.
items.why: “Did not involve the child” and stigmatising language are both failing statements.
items.fix: Speak to Kai first — how he is, whether anyone teases him — and use health-focused words.

items.fail: Calculating an adult BMI or quoting adult cut-offs.
items.why: NICE NG246 uses BMI centiles on UK90 charts for children; adult thresholds are wrong.
items.fix: “We plot him on a chart for his age” — and arrange a proper measurement.

items.fail: No screen for secondary causes or comorbidity.
items.why: Examiners expect you to ask about height pattern, development, snoring, joints and mood.
items.fix: Four quick questions: height and growth, development, snoring, joints — then blood pressure at the nurse visit.

items.fail: Giving a diet sheet or calorie target for a 9-year-old.
items.why: NICE NG246 favours family-based, multicomponent change; restricting one child reinforces shame.
items.fix: Let the family choose one or two small changes, and refer to a family programme.

items.why: Bullying is a harm in its own right and a barrier to activity; missing it is a missed cue.
items.fix: Acknowledge it at once, return to it in the plan, and offer to contact school with consent.

timeMap.d: Let her vent. Then, early and clearly: not a bad mum, no diet. Ask permission to talk about it.
Ask Kai about school and teasing. Snoring, joints, tiredness. Height pattern and development. A normal family day, without judgement.
What went through her mind at the letter; what she wants from today.
Centiles, not adult BMI. Measure and BP this week. Family’s own one or two changes. Family programme. School and school nurse about bullying.
Recap; snoring, limp, thirst, low mood. Reaffirm the alliance.

wordPics.fail: Uses the word “fat” or lectures about diet in front of Kai; applies adult BMI; blames the mother; gives a calorie target; never asks Kai how he is or about bullying; no plan or follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Removes blame, explains centiles, arranges measurement and blood pressure, screens for secondary causes and comorbidity, and agrees family-based changes with a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: turns anger into alliance by naming her goal for Kai’s happiness; asks Kai directly about teasing and acts on it; lets the family choose the changes; uses Kai’s love of football; signposts a family programme without the word “diet”; both leave hopeful.

avoid.dont: “Kai is obese and needs to lose weight.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s look at how Kai is growing on a chart for his age, and think about what helps him feel his best.”
avoid.why: Labels and weight-loss targets in front of a child shame him and end engagement.

avoid.dont: “He needs to cut out snacks and eat less.”
avoid.instead: “What’s one change the whole family could try that would feel easy?”
avoid.why: Individual restriction for a child is not the NICE NG246 approach; family-based change is.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, lots of kids are big at this age.”
avoid.instead: “The letter is a snapshot — let’s measure him properly and look at the pattern.”
avoid.why: False reassurance avoids the conversation the family came to have.

You came in because you care about him. We’re on the same side.

SCA_STEM.name: Kai Pyle
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Letter from the school measurement programme describing Kai’s weight as very overweight. Mother, Mrs Donna Pyle, booked the appointment; Kai is with her.
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother upset by the letter; wants to discuss it.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG246 (2025) — Overweight and obesity management · NICE CG89 — Child maltreatment: when to suspect · National Child Measurement Programme (Office for Health Improvement and Disparities)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: In children, weight is judged by BMI centile for age and sex, not adult cut-offs. Most childhood obesity reflects family-wide habits; secondary causes are rare and usually come with short stature or developmental delay. The management is family-based, positive and free of blame.

points.t: NICE NG246: use BMI centiles on UK90 charts in children, not adult BMI. Overweight is at or above the 91st centile; obesity at or above the 98th centile. Plot height and weight and look at the trajectory.

points.h: Look for a cause only when the pattern suggests one
points.t: Short stature or slowing height velocity, developmental delay, dysmorphic features, or very early-onset severe obesity suggest an endocrine or genetic cause and need paediatric assessment. A child who is growing along or above his height centile is reassuring.

NICE NG246: consider assessing comorbidities at or above the 98th centile — blood pressure, glucose and lipids, snoring and sleep apnoea, joint problems, acanthosis nigricans, and psychological wellbeing including bullying and low self-esteem.

NICE NG246: family-based, multicomponent lifestyle interventions — diet, physical activity and behaviour change — are the core. For many growing children the aim is to slow weight gain while height catches up, not to diet.
Use neutral, person-first language focused on health; avoid blame and avoid words that stigmatise, especially with the child present. Ask permission before discussing weight.
Weight alone is not a safeguarding issue. NICE CG89 applies only where there are wider concerns about neglect, such as failure to engage with care for serious obesity-related harm.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let the mother vent about the letter; acknowledged the child in the room.
Busy family routines, screen time, transport, cost and time barriers, bullying at school, the mother’s feelings of judgement.
Picked up “now he’s upset” and Kai’s “sometimes” about teasing, and the mother’s fear of him obsessing about food.
Idea (he’s just a growing boy); concern (judged as a bad mother, a child on a diet); expectation (to know if he is alright).
Height, weight and BMI centile on UK90 charts; blood pressure; bloods only if the centile or history warrants.
Lifestyle-related obesity versus endocrine or genetic causes (short stature, delay, dysmorphism) and comorbidities.
Snoring and apnoeas, hip or knee pain and limp, thirst and tiredness, growth pattern, mood and bullying.
Probable overweight or obesity on the school measurement, to be confirmed by centile and trajectory; no features of a secondary cause.
Family-chosen small changes; family-based programme referral per NICE NG246; no restrictive diet; review with measurements.
Bullying addressed with school and school nurse; comorbidity assessment if at or above the 98th centile.
Nurse measurement this week and review; named symptoms for sleep apnoea, SUFE, diabetes and low mood.

social.t: Children living with obesity are often teased. Bullying harms mental health and reduces activity; it deserves its own plan with school.
Time pressure, cost of food and activities, and access to safe places to play shape what is achievable. Ask, and fit the plan to the family.

legal.t: NICE CG89: obesity alone is not a safeguarding concern. Consider neglect only where there are wider concerns, such as persistent failure to engage with care for serious obesity-related harm.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): ask the parent’s agreement before contacting school about bullying, and share only what is needed.
Person-first, health-focused language and asking permission to discuss weight are part of treating patients with respect (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

community.t: Local family-based child weight-management programmes (tier 2) and the school nurse; the National Child Measurement Programme letter usually lists local support.

redFlags: Short stature, falling height centile, developmental delay or dysmorphism — endocrine or genetic cause, paediatric assessment
Loud snoring with apnoeas, hip or knee pain with a limp (SUFE), thirst and polyuria
Low mood, bullying, self-harm or disordered eating
psychosocial: Family routines: meals, drinks, screens, transport, sleep
Kai’s experience at school and his self-esteem
ice: Idea: “He’s just a growing boy — the letter is wrong”
Concern: being judged as a bad mother; Kai being put on a diet or obsessing about food
Expectation: to know whether he is actually alright

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Possible overweight or obesity on a school measurement, to be confirmed by BMI centile on UK90 charts with height trajectory. No features of a secondary cause; comorbidity assessment if at or above the 98th centile.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “For children we don’t use the adult measure. We plot height and weight on a chart for his age, and what matters is how he’s tracking over time — not one number in a letter.”

management.reflectIce: “You want Kai to be happy and relaxed about food — that’s exactly our goal too. Nobody here is judging you as a mum.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around the family’s time and budget, Kai’s love of football, and the bullying, which needs its own action with school.
sharedPlan: Nurse appointment: height, weight, BMI centile on UK90 charts, blood pressure
One or two family-chosen changes (water instead of fizzy drinks; more football)
Referral to a family weight-management programme; school and school nurse about teasing
safetyNet: Snoring with pauses in breathing, limp or hip or knee pain, thirst or tiredness — come back sooner
Low mood or worsening bullying — tell us; review after the measurements

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed on words, not knowledge. A candidate who knows the centile thresholds still fails if the mother feels blamed or Kai hears himself described as fat.

items.fail: Arguing with the mother about whether the letter is right.
items.why: Defending the school puts you on the opposite side; the anger is shame and fear of judgement.
items.fix: Name her feelings, say clearly she is not a bad mum, and ask permission to talk about it.

items.fail: Talking about Kai’s weight in the third person while he sits there.
items.why: “Did not involve the child” and stigmatising language are both failing statements.
items.fix: Speak to Kai first — how he is, whether anyone teases him — and use health-focused words.

items.fail: Calculating an adult BMI or quoting adult cut-offs.
items.why: NICE NG246 uses BMI centiles on UK90 charts for children; adult thresholds are wrong.
items.fix: “We plot him on a chart for his age” — and arrange a proper measurement.

items.fail: No screen for secondary causes or comorbidity.
items.why: Examiners expect you to ask about height pattern, development, snoring, joints and mood.
items.fix: Four quick questions: height and growth, development, snoring, joints — then blood pressure at the nurse visit.

items.fail: Giving a diet sheet or calorie target for a 9-year-old.
items.why: NICE NG246 favours family-based, multicomponent change; restricting one child reinforces shame.
items.fix: Let the family choose one or two small changes, and refer to a family programme.

items.why: Bullying is a harm in its own right and a barrier to activity; missing it is a missed cue.
items.fix: Acknowledge it at once, return to it in the plan, and offer to contact school with consent.
